gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured power draw for any NAS that could host WordPress. Dong Knows Tech measured the Synology DS225+ at about 275 Wh per 24 hours with two hard drives, an average of about 11.5 W. At the EIA's 2026 US residential average of 18.19¢/kWh, running it all year costs about $18, below the floor of ChatGPT's unsourced '$20–60 incremental' electricity range. QNAP's own typical figure for the TS-264 (29.086 W) works out to about $46 a year.
standout_why: ChatGPT ran no search and got no results, so there is no cited rival page. Its answer estimates electricity at '$20–60 incremental' a year with no source or model. It names no reviewer, no wattage and no per-model figure, and it does not say that drive type (SSD or HDD) and spin-down move the bill several-fold. Our current page's 'about $1 a month power' for the DXP2800 also has no named measurement behind it.
decides: This confirms that power is not the reason to choose paid hosting. Measured or typical draw puts a year of electricity for a 2-bay NAS at about $9–46: DXP2800 about $9–23, DS225+ about $18, TS-264 about $29–46 on QNAP's own figures. That is about the same as a first-year Hostinger plan ($1.99 × 12 = $23.88) or below a $4-a-month DigitalOcean droplet ($48 a year). The deciding factors stay uptime, security and upload bandwidth, not the electric bill. Among the candidates, the measured figures favour the low-draw N100 DXP2800 and the DS225+ over the TS-264 for a box that runs 24/7. Our current 'about $1 a month' for the DXP2800 matches Ocinside's ~7 W idle (about $0.93 a month).

findings.label: Measured energy use per 24 hours (two hard drives installed)
findings.source_title: Synology DS225+ review – Dong Knows Tech (Dong Ngo), published 2025-07-23, full review 2025-08-04
findings.note: Spec table: 'Power Consumption (per 24 hours) ≈ 275 Wh (tested with two hard drives)'. Measurement method and drive models for the power test are not stated. 275 Wh ÷ 24 h = 11.46 W. 275 Wh × 365 = 100.4 kWh a year × $0.1819/kWh (EIA 2026 YTD) = $18.26 a year for the whole box, not just the extra load.

findings.label: Synology's rated power (as repeated by NASCompares)
findings.value: 16.98 W during access; 6.08 W in HDD hibernation
findings.source_title: Synology DS225+ NAS Review – Should You Buy? – NASCompares (Rob Andrews), 2025-08-04
findings.note: These are Synology's spec figures, not NASCompares' own meter readings; the article does not describe a measurement. 16.98 W × 8.76 = 148.7 kWh a year = $27.05; 6.08 W × 8.76 = 53.3 kWh = $9.69.

findings.label: Wall-socket power, Igor'sLab test (one NVMe SSD, hard drives removed)
findings.value: 0.6 W off (WoL on); 5.6 W standby; 14.5 W during data transfer
findings.source_title: UGREEN NASync DXP2800 NAS im Test – Igor'sLab (Tim Kutzner), 2024-05-08, updated 2025-05-31
findings.note: Measured at the wall with only one NVMe SSD; the meter is not named. Igor'sLab notes that draw depends mainly on the drives. 5.6 W × 8.76 = 49.1 kWh a year = $8.92; 14.5 W × 8.76 = 127.0 kWh = $23.11 at 18.19¢. This SSD-only setup suits a WordPress volume.

findings.label: Idle and maximum power, Ocinside test (3.5-inch HDDs in RAID 1)
findings.source_title: Ugreen DXP2800 NAS Review – ocinside.de (Redaktion ocinside.de), page 4
findings.note: The page is undated and has no byline. The maximum is a combined CPU, RAM and HDD stress test; drive models and meter are not named. 7 W × 8.76 = 61.3 kWh a year = $11.15 (about $0.93 a month), which supports our page's 'about $1 a month'.

findings.product: UGREEN NASync DXP2800 GT (sibling model, AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514, not the N100 DXP2800 we list)
findings.label: Idle and load power, Notebookcheck (two WD Red HDDs)
findings.value: 14.84–20.14 W idle; 31.12 W full CPU load; 35.9 W maximum with CPU and drives loaded
findings.source_title: Small, fast and surprisingly quiet: Ugreen NASync DXP2800 GT review – Notebookcheck (Daniel Schmidt), 2026-10-13
findings.note: This is a different model, kept only as context so it is not mixed up with the DXP2800. Idle means drives spinning with no file activity. 14.84–20.14 W × 8.76 = 130.0–176.4 kWh a year = $23.65–$32.09.

findings.label: QNAP's rated power (drives fully populated)
findings.note: This is QNAP's own spec figure, not an independent measurement; it says 'Tested with drives fully populated' without naming the drives. CPU: Celeron N5095, 8 GB DDR4. 29.086 W × 8.76 = 254.8 kWh a year = $46.35; 18.288 W × 8.76 = 160.2 kWh = $29.14 at 18.19¢.

findings.label: US average residential electricity price
findings.value: 18.19¢/kWh 2026 year to date (18.16¢ in August 2026; 17.23¢ for full-year 2025)
findings.source_title: EIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.3 – Average Price of Electricity to Ultimate Customers (data for August 2026, released 2026-10-23)
findings.note: 2026 values are preliminary. This is the rate used for every per-year cost above (W × 8.76 = kWh a year).

unsourced: QNAP TS-264 independent measured idle and active power: Toshiba's HDD lab report TSH209 (toshiba-storage.com/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/TOSHIBA_HDD_LabReport_TSH209_QNAP_web.pdf) appears to list 1.6 W / 27.0 W / 33.0 W with two N300 8TB drives. The PDF could not be read as text, and the HTML summary pages (toshiba-storage.com/?p=66352, toshiba.semicon-storage.com TSH209 page) give no figures or column labels, so I left it out.
Trusted Reviews' 13 W peak for the DS225+ (with WD drives): only seen quoted on aggregators (starryhope.com, smarthomeexplorer.com); the Trusted Reviews article itself did not turn up.

Any named benchmark of WordPress running on a NAS (TTFB, requests per second or concurrent users) for the DXP2800, DS225+ or TS-264: searched for Synology/NAS WordPress load tests and found only shared-hosting benchmarks. NASCompares and Dong Knows Tech test file transfer only.

A named median US fixed-broadband upload speed (Ookla H1 2026 US Connectivity Report): ookla.com and speedtest.net blocked fetching. The IEEE ComSoc summary (2026-07-23) gives only AT&T Fiber's 320.65 Mbps median upload, not a national or cable figure.
